title: Where Touch Is First Processed: Dorsal Horn and Dorsal Column Nuclei

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: In the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, the second-order axon crosses in the {{c1::medulla}}.
cards.quote: The second-order axon crosses in the medulla and reaches the ventral posterolateral thalamus (VPL).
cards.section: Two routes on one drawing

cards.front: What carries touch information along the direct dorsal column route to the gracile nucleus?
cards.back: The primary touch afferent's own axon; it ascends without a spinal synapse.
cards.quote: Its main branch climbs the dorsal column to the gracile nucleus with no synapse on the way.
cards.section: Two routes on one drawing

cards.front: What makes a spinal neuron a postsynaptic dorsal column (PSDC) neuron?
cards.back: It receives input in the dorsal horn and sends its own axon up the dorsal column to the dorsal column nuclei.
cards.quote: a spinal neuron that receives input in the dorsal horn and sends an axon up the dorsal column to the DCN.
cards.section: Two routes on one drawing

cards.front: How can a low-threshold mechanoreceptor class with no direct branch to the gracile nucleus still contribute to ascending touch signals?
cards.back: Through spinal circuits that drive postsynaptic dorsal column neurons, whose axons ascend to the dorsal column nuclei.
cards.quote: Other LTMR classes have no direct branch to the gracile nucleus; they can contribute through spinal circuits.
cards.section: Two routes on one drawing

cards.front: A mouse gracile neuron receives both direct afferent and indirect spinal input. Design a comparison that distinguishes their contributions rather than just showing that both exist.
cards.back: Record its stimulus responses with both routes intact, then silence direct afferent terminals in the gracile nucleus and block lumbar synapses separately. Compare the response components lost with each manipulation. This uses selective removal to assign each route a contribution.
cards.quote: Take one route away at a time and see what the neuron loses:
cards.section: Two routes on one drawing

cards.front: How did Turecek and colleagues silence direct input while sparing the afferents' spinal branches in adult anaesthetized mice?
cards.back: They activated the light-gated chloride channel ACR1 at afferent terminals in the gracile nucleus, leaving the branches in the cord outside the illumination.
cards.quote: The light was aimed at the gracile nucleus, sparing the afferents' branches in the cord.
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: Why could lumbar glutamate receptor antagonists suppress indirect input while direct afferent conduction continued in the mouse experiment?
cards.back: The antagonists blocked spinal synapses driving PSDC neurons; the direct ascending afferent branches have no spinal synapse to block.
cards.quote: the afferents' ascending branches, which have no synapse on their way up the dorsal column, keep conducting.
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: A neuron's receptive field is the {{c1::patch of skin}} whose touch drives it.
cards.quote: a receptive field is the patch of skin whose touch drives the neuron
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: What did aligned direct and indirect receptive fields on single mouse VPL-projecting gracile neurons imply?
cards.back: The routes reported the same skin patch with complementary information, converging on individual brainstem neurons.
cards.quote: So the two routes are not two maps but two reports on one spot, meeting on one neuron.
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: In a hypothetical adult anaesthetized mouse recording, lumbar synaptic blockade leaves vibration timing intact but eliminates sustained pressure firing. What dependence does this reveal?
cards.back: Sustained firing depends on lumbar synaptic transmission, while the preserved vibration timing does not. Direct afferent conduction remains available; the result does not identify a PSDC-specific mechanism.
cards.quote: To remove the indirect route, they applied glutamate receptor antagonists to the lumbar cord.
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: Why would extrapolating the mouse ACR1 terminal-silencing result to strong indentations exceed the validated experiment?
cards.back: ACR1 silencing was validated only at about 20 to 30 mN or less. The high-force conclusion instead rests on lumbar drug blockade, which was not PSDC-specific.
cards.quote: ACR1 silencing was validated only for gentle stimuli, about 20 to 30 mN or less
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: In adult anaesthetized mice, would removing direct afferent input necessarily abolish all responses to gentle skin displacement? What happens and why?
cards.back: Not necessarily: a contribution can remain through the indirect route. Both routes contributed to gentle displacement, so it is not carried exclusively by direct input.
cards.quote: both routes contributed to gentle displacement, so "direct means vibration and indirect means light touch" is too simple.
cards.section: The key experiment: silence one route at a time

cards.front: For an axon of length L conducting at constant speed v, conduction time t = {{c1::L / v}}.
cards.quote: The model assumes constant velocity, conduction plus synaptic delay only
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: In an illustrative model, direct input travels 0.08 m at 16 m/s. Indirect input travels 0.04 m at 16 m/s, crosses two 1 ms spinal synapses, then travels 0.04 m at 8 m/s. Matched final synaptic delays cancel. What is the indirect lag?
cards.back: Direct: (0.08/16) × 1000 = 5.0 ms. Indirect: (0.04/16) × 1000 + 2 × 1 + (0.04/8) × 1000 = 9.5 ms. Lag: 9.5 − 5.0 = 4.5 ms. These are model values, not measured latencies.
cards.quote: The indirect input arrives about 4.5 ms later in this model.
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: With equal cord-to-brainstem path lengths, matched final synapses, and an indirect axon no faster than the direct afferent, why must a spinal relay arrive later?
cards.back: It cannot recover time through faster conduction, and its added spinal synapses introduce additional delay.
cards.quote: with a PSDC axon no faster than the afferent, the spinal synapses alone make the indirect input later.
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: An illustrative indirect route lags by 4.5 ms during a 300 ms press. What percentage of the press is that, and does this alone establish a negligible perceptual effect?
cards.back: (4.5 ms / 300 ms) × 100 = 1.5%. No: this fraction does not establish effects on onset detection, integration, or perception; it only compares durations.
cards.quote: 4.5 ms is 1.5 percent of the press, though that fraction says nothing about onset detection, integration with other inputs or perception.
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: For a 500 Hz vibration, express a fixed 4.5 ms delay in cycles and give its phase shift within one cycle.
cards.back: Period = 1000/500 = 2.0 ms. Delay = 4.5/2.0 = 2.25 cycles. The fractional 0.25 cycle gives 0.25 × 360° = 90°.
cards.quote: At 500 Hz, 2.25 cycles shifts the locked phase by a quarter cycle (90°)
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: Why can a fixed relay delay preserve vibration phase locking while variable relay delay blurs it?
cards.back: A fixed delay moves every spike to the same new phase. Variable delay scatters spikes across phases, weakening locking.
cards.quote: A fixed delay does not blur one route's own locking: if every spike is late by the same amount, the spikes still share one phase.
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: What does vector strength measure for a neuron responding to vibration?
cards.back: How tightly spikes lock to one phase: 1 means all share one phase; 0 means no net phase preference.
cards.quote: Vector strength is a locking score: how tightly spikes lock to one phase of a vibration cycle
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: In the toy jitter model, direct timing has σ = 0.2 ms and two spinal synapses each add independent jitter with σ = 0.5 ms. What is the indirect timing spread?
cards.back: Independent variances add: σ = √[(0.2 ms)² + (0.5 ms)² + (0.5 ms)²] = √0.54 ms² ≈ 0.73 ms. These spreads are assumptions, not measurements.
cards.quote: Independent spreads add as squares, so the indirect route has σ = √(0.2² + 0.5² + 0.5²) ≈ 0.73 ms.
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: A toy model adds independent spinal jitter. Lower vibration frequencies retain locking better than higher frequencies. Does this establish why the indirect mouse route lacks precise high-frequency timing? What follows and why?
cards.back: It establishes a possible mechanism, not the experimental explanation. The rule is that timing variability scatters phase more at higher frequency, but the jitter values were assumed and relays need not add that much.
cards.quote: the model shows a possibility, not the paper's explanation:
cards.section: What a slower route costs

cards.front: Receiving input from more than one kind of afferent is called {{c1::convergence}}.
cards.quote: They found convergence, one neuron receiving input from more than one kind of afferent
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: How does feedforward inhibition make an excitatory input recruit inhibition of the same target neuron?
cards.back: The input excites both the target and an inhibitory interneuron; the interneuron then inhibits the target, so inhibition follows excitation.
cards.quote: The same afferent input that excites a PSDC neuron also excites an interneuron that inhibits it, so excitation is followed by inhibition.
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: At what site does presynaptic inhibition reduce an afferent's influence, and how?
cards.back: At the afferent terminal, by scaling down transmitter release.
cards.quote: Inhibition is applied to the afferent terminal, scaling down the transmitter it releases.
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: Which interneurons supplied glycinergic feedforward inhibition onto mouse PSDC neurons in Chirila and colleagues' study?
cards.back: Rorβ interneurons.
cards.quote: Rorβ interneurons supplied glycinergic feedforward inhibition onto PSDC neurons.
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: Based on the adult anaesthetized mouse PSDC recordings, what happens to the skin area driving a neuron when either feedforward or presynaptic inhibition is disrupted, and why?
cards.back: It expands: touches farther from the field centre can drive firing because inhibitory restriction of the receptive field has been weakened.
cards.quote: Disrupting either motif enlarged PSDC receptive fields: a larger field means touches farther from its centre now drive the neuron.
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: In the adult anaesthetized mouse PSDC experiment, what abnormal response may follow the end of a step indentation when presynaptic inhibition is lost?
cards.back: Firing may continue after the indentation ends: loss of presynaptic inhibition produced after-discharge.
cards.quote: Loss of presynaptic inhibition also produced after-discharge, continued firing after the end of a step indentation.
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: A chronic conditional knockout changes an adult neural circuit's responses. What further manipulation would help distinguish an immediate circuit role from effects accumulated during development?
cards.back: Disrupt the same function acutely in adults and compare the response change. The rule is that chronic disruption can alter wiring, so a chronic phenotype alone cannot isolate acute circuit function.
cards.quote: both disruptions were chronic conditional knockouts
cards.section: What the dorsal horn does to the signal

cards.front: Where is the LTMR recipient zone in the mouse lumbar dorsal horn?
cards.back: A band in the middle of the dorsal horn, beginning just below the IB4-labelled band of a subset of nociceptor terminals.
cards.quote: LTMRs end in a band in the middle of the dorsal horn, the LTMR recipient zone (LTMR-RZ).
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: A reporter-defined neuronal population is marked by a {{c1::gene it expresses}}, which does not prove that it is one cell type.
cards.quote: A reporter-defined population is one marked in a mouse line by a gene it expresses, which is a molecular label, not proof of a single cell type
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: Why is Abraira and colleagues' seven-excitatory, four-inhibitory population atlas of the mouse LTMR recipient zone incomplete?
cards.back: The reporter lines together covered an estimated 71 to 82 percent of neurons in the zone, leaving some unrepresented.
cards.quote: The reporter lines together covered an estimated 71 to 82 percent of LTMR-RZ neurons, so the atlas is incomplete.
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: Why does the mouse LTMR recipient-zone atlas argue against each afferent class having a private interneuron line?
cards.back: Each assayed LTMR subtype contacted four to eleven interneuron subtypes; interneuron subtypes sampled one to three assayed LTMR classes. The contacts support mixing, rather than private lines.
cards.quote: each LTMR subtype assayed contacted four to eleven interneuron subtypes, and each interneuron subtype sampled one to three of the LTMR classes assayed
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: After a neural manipulation, animals stop preferring a newly textured object. They still prefer objects with novel colour and shape in the same recognition task. What alternative explanation does that control weaken?
cards.back: A general failure to explore or recognize objects. The retained non-texture preference supports a texture-related deficit, rather than a general loss of object exploration or recognition.
cards.quote: The silenced mice kept the preference, so the deficit is not a general failure to explore or recognize objects.
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: Why does silencing a spinal marker lineage in the mouse texture task fail to show that every currently marker-positive subtype is necessary?
cards.back: A lineage includes all cells that ever expressed the marker, so the manipulation is neither acute nor restricted to one pure current cell type.
cards.quote: a lineage includes every cell that ever expressed the marker, so the silencing is not acute and not one pure type.
cards.section: Who is in the zone: an atlas

cards.front: What is allodynia?
cards.back: Pain from normally non-painful touch.
cards.quote: An enlarged PSDC receptive field is not allodynia (pain from normally non-painful touch)
cards.section: When inhibition fails

cards.front: Silencing direct afferent terminals reduces surround suppression in mouse gracile neurons. Does that prove a fully mapped inhibitory microcircuit?
cards.back: No. It supports direct input recruiting local inhibition, because removing that input weakens suppression. The rule is that a perturbation reveals a contribution, but this experiment did not resolve the full microcircuit.
cards.quote: Silencing the direct afferent terminals reduced that surround suppression, which points to direct input acting mainly through local inhibitory neurons of the nucleus
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: Suppose an acute reduction of afferent presynaptic inhibition enlarges PSDC receptive fields in awake adult mice and impairs tactile acuity. What additional intervention would test whether PSDC output mediates the behavioural effect?
cards.back: Add a perturbation or rescue restricted to PSDC output and assess tactile acuity with a non-texture control. The rule is that a broad spinal change alone does not establish PSDC-specific causation.
cards.quote: Add a perturbation or rescue restricted to PSDC output.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Would a mouse spinal-inhibition effect on tactile acuity establish the same perceptual mechanism in people? What experiment would begin to test transfer?
cards.back: No. Pair human psychophysical acuity measurements with a safe way to change spinal inhibition. The rule is that mouse findings do not transfer by default; any human conclusion remains limited to the tested preparation.
cards.quote: In people, you would need psychophysical acuity measures and a way to change spinal inhibition safely
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does parvalbumin expression alone fail to classify a neuron as inhibitory in the mouse LTMR recipient-zone atlas?
cards.back: The atlas includes an excitatory parvalbumin population, PVe, as well as an inhibitory one, PVi.
cards.quote: Parvalbumin is not an inhibitory marker by default here: PVe is excitatory and PVi is inhibitory.
cards.section: The interneuron populations and their firing patterns

cards.front: In fixed mouse tissue, mean axo-axonic inhibitory contacts per sensory terminal were 2.9 overall and 1.5 from PVi neurons. What percentage were PVi contacts, and does that give the percentage of inhibition?
cards.back: (1.5 / 2.9) × 100 ≈ 52% of counted contacts. No: contact counts do not measure conductance, so this does not establish the fraction of functional inhibition.
cards.quote: These are contact counts, not conductances, so they do not say PVi neurons supply half of the inhibition.
cards.section: Counting inhibitory contacts
